articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Components for Novel Transmission Lines' (Digest No.048)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Components for Novel Transmission Lines
IEE Colloquium on Components for Novel Transmission Lines
abstract: Inset Dielectric Guide (IDG), which is simply a rectangular slot filled with dielectric material, was proposed as a practical evolution from Image Line with the potential for easier manufacture and improved performance. IDG as an antenna medium seems to offer particular promise. It is easy to lay thin metal strips on the air-dielectric interface that act as dipole radiators to form integrated leaky wave arrays. Following the successful design and realization of a 23-element vertically polarized array in a deep slot, this paper presents a novel 15-element array with horizontal polarization.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A broadband single-sideband mixer with low spurious levels
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Components for Novel Transmission Lines
abstract: A miniature image rejection mixer has been made which covers the KA Band. It is in suspended microstrip form using quartz substrates for durability. The local oscillator is applied to a fin-line port resulting in low spurious outputs. A novel microstrip to fin-line transition is used.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A prospect for telephony and other domestic communications on gas and water pipe networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Components for Novel Transmission Lines
abstract: The characteristics of local telephone cables limit the performance of domestic communications. Replacement with fibre-optic cables for residential property has been deemed uneconomic, and there is no clear alternative to the 50 volts 600 ohm pair. However, changes in the metering of domestic services for water and gas provides scope for a high speed digital communication circuit on the pipe networks. The modern material for underground pipework is polyethylene, and the technique for laying sizes between 1" and 30" in long lengths is established. The inclusion of wires and strips of metallic conductors within the wall of the pipe during extrusion is practicable, and techniques are already established for the electrical welding of joints and junctions in the field, and these can be extended to cover such electrical circuits. Thus a path is available between each individual house and a kiosk at the end of the street where connections can easily be made to the fibre-optic trunk network of the telephone system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multi-level transmission line circuits for MMICs
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Components for Novel Transmission Lines
abstract: Even since their conception in the 1970s, GaAs MMICs have used conventional microstripline techniques. The semi-insulating GaAs substrate is used to confine the field around the conductors, with the back face metalised and grounded. The microstriplines' widths scale directly with the chip thickness, so that 100 mu m and 200 mu m is usually used to allow a reasonable range of line impedances and widths. With such wide conductors, however, the gaps between lines must be enormous to prevent coupling problems. In addition, for operation above around 12 GHz, devices and components can only be effectively grounded with through-GaAs via-hole technology. This technology is expensive, and limits the maximum wafer size that can be handled safely, because of the extra fragility. This limit on wafer diameter is the biggest problem for keeping chip costs down. In addition, at millimetric frequencies the via-hole inductance becomes significant. Because of these problems with conventional microstrip circuits, there is now a lot of interest in using coplanar waveguide instead, particularly in Japan. Coplanar waveguide does not use a grounded backface, and its dimensions do not depend much on the substrate thickness; thus via-holes are eliminated and a chip thickness of 600 mu m is acceptable. The wafer diameter can be increased significantly, yielding many more chips per wafer and reducing their cost. The major disadvantage of CPW is that the ground planes must go wherever the signal conductor goes; in a simple amplifier this is not a problem, but in a complex multi-function chip the interconnection problems are impossible to solve neatly. There is a potential solution to all these problems. In addition to using coplanar techniques, one can add additional metal layers and dielectric layers to the basic GaAs CPW. This gives the circuit designer the ability to use a new family of basic transmission-line types.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Ferrite loaded transmission lines for high voltage pulse-sharpening
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Components for Novel Transmission Lines
abstract: This work is concerned with the concept of pulse sharpening in ferrite loaded co-axial lines particularly as the result of nonlinearity in the propagation medium causing a change in the magnetic permeability with the passage of an electromagnetic wavefront.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Components for Novel Transmission Lines
abstract: The use of dielectric waveguides for high microwave frequencies in place of metallic rectangular waveguides has been suggested for many years. Besides the problems of manufacturing very small metallic rectangular waveguides for use above 90 GHz and the increasing attenuation due to the skin effect and surface roughness there is also the problem of attenuation and repeatability in the connectors. This latter problem is particularly acute when measurements are made using standard impedances. Following the successful six-port reflectometer made in dielectric guide the next project at Kent involves a multistate reflectometer in dielectric guide. A multistate reflectometer has the advantage over a six-port reflectometer in that it requires two less power meters. In order to achieve this, the device also needs a means of changing phase. This present paper describes a novel broadband phase shifter which has been designed for use in multistate reflectometer. The whole device will then enable the user to make very accurate measurements of phase and amplitude in the range 70-140 GHz for not very much more than the cost of a swept source.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Improved manufacturing method for millimetre wave components
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Components for Novel Transmission Lines
abstract: In developing integrated components for application in the 26-40 GHz band much of the early work in the field has concentrated on hybrid circuits built in quartz microstrip. Quartz was selected because of its favourable dielectric properties. The question which arises, however, is whether that material is the most suitable for routine production of microwave components. In this paper alternative materials are considered which have been shown to be suitable for production and which have good microwave performance. The paper discusses the alternative materials which are available and then goes on to describe some millimetre wave components which have been built with soft substrate technology. Performance figures are given and the advantages of using this approach are highlighted.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
